title: Ways of saying
grammar: Advanced verb patterns (verb + object + to-infinitive / -ing; reporting verbs; verbs of perception)

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: How we report what others say changes everything. Master advanced verb patterns and say exactly what you mean.
scene.intro: Communication is trickier than it looks. A single reporting verb can accuse, excuse or forgive; a verb of perception can turn a debate into a quarrel. In this unit you explore how we retell what others say, and you master the advanced verb patterns that C1 English demands — verb plus object plus infinitive or -ing, reporting verbs and verbs of perception. You will also practise the open cloze from Part 2. For the Inspiring Nordic project, saying it accurately is everything. Let's begin.

activities.title: Reading — the reading club on communication

data.title: Ways of saying
data.author: nadia
data.text:
How often have you meant one thing and been understood to say another? Communication, it turns out, is far less reliable than we like to believe. We do not simply exchange words; we interpret, we report, and in reporting we quietly reshape.

Consider the humble reporting verb. If I tell you that Mateo admitted forgetting his homework, you picture guilt. If I say he explained that he had forgotten it, you feel sympathy. The event is identical; only the verb has changed. In our Grade 11 club we spent a whole session watching how a single word can accuse, excuse or forgive.

Verbs of perception play a similar game. When Liam said he heard Sofía arguing with a teacher, the class assumed a conflict — yet what he had actually seen was a lively debate about a poem. We hear people doing things and instantly build a story around them.

Then there are the verbs that carry instructions. Parents warn us not to stay out late; friends persuade us to take risks; teachers advise us to think twice. Each pattern — verb plus object plus infinitive or -ing — encodes an attitude as much as an action.

The lesson for the Inspiring Nordic project is sobering. Before we report what a tradesperson or an expert has told us, we should ask whether our chosen verbs are faithful or merely convenient. To misquote is easy; to represent someone accurately is a genuine skill. As Nadia reminded the club, the way of saying is never neutral.

data.title: Advanced verb patterns
data.intro: Many verbs are followed by a particular pattern, and the pattern carries meaning. Learn which verbs take an object + to-infinitive, which take -ing, and how reporting and perception verbs behave.

examples.text: The teacher advised us to rewrite the essay.
We heard Sofía singing in the hall.
They warned us not to be late.

rules: persuade, advise, warn, encourage, remind + object + to-infinitive: They encouraged me to apply.
admit, deny, suggest, recommend + -ing: She suggested leaving early.
see, hear, watch, feel + object + -ing (action in progress) or bare infinitive (whole action): I saw him fall.

items.sentence: We heard someone ___ in the next room.
The sign warns visitors ___ the animals.

activities.title: Use of English Part 2 — open cloze. Write ONE word in each gap.

data.text: Communication often goes wrong. We assume that others think {1} we do, and then we blame them {2} the confusion. Nadia warned us not {3} jump to conclusions. When someone reports {4} another person said, the meaning can quietly shift. What matters is listening, {5} we rarely do carefully enough. Only then {6} we begin to understand each other.

activities.title: Listening — the reporting-verbs lesson. Write ONE word in each gap.

data.voice_note: Voz: la profesora (Miss Vega), sobre los reporting verbs.
data.script: Good morning, Grade 11. Today we look at reporting verbs and the way we retell what people say. Notice how a single verb changes everything: he admitted lying, she denied cheating, they suggested leaving. Small choices, big meanings. For homework, listen to a real conversation and report three sentences using different verbs. Nadia will share her examples first on Friday. Remember: verbs of perception like watch and hear take an object plus an -ing form. Bring your sharpest ear, and report what you hear precisely.

activities.title: Speaking — retell a conversation. In pairs, then record it.

data.text: In pairs, retell a recent conversation, choosing your reporting verbs carefully. Model: “She admitted forgetting, but I suspect she simply chose not to reply.” 1) When was the last time you were badly misunderstood? 2) Do we report gossip more accurately than facts? 3) Which reporting verb — admit, deny, claim, insist — is most often abused in the news? Give reasons and examples, then record your discussion.

homework.prompt: Write a short account (10–12 sentences) of a real misunderstanding, reporting what each person said with a range of verb patterns (advised… to…, admitted …-ing, warned… not to…, heard… -ing). Capital letters and full stops!
